summaries.summary: NMT has improved translation quality, uses encoder-decoder architectures, and attentional NMT is popular for using relevant source parts and translating longer sentences.
Figure FIGREF1 illustrates attention using relevant source words, while the paper studies smeared attention cases like “would” and “like”.
Prior work modified attention, compared it with traditional word alignment, trained attention with alignments, and viewed attention as reordering and alignment.
The paper investigates differences between attention and alignment, asking whether attention only models alignment and how similarity varies across syntactic phenomena.
Analysis shows attention closely matches traditional alignments for nouns but captures information beyond translational equivalents for verbs.
Contributions include comparing attention and word alignment, showing compliance effects, word-type patterns, and context-word attention explaining differences from alignment.
Related work trains attention with GIZA++ and fast_align alignments, reports mixed translation gains, separates alignment and translation models, and uses HMM/IBM alignments.
shi-padhi-knight:2016:EMNLP2016 find syntactic information in encoder hidden states, while belinkov2017neural show attention improves source-side POS tag learning.
koehn2017six briefly analyzed attention-alignment matching across languages using probability mass over automatic alignments and differences based on most attended words.
Mixed results from chen2016guided, alkhouli-EtAl:2016:WMT, and liu-EtAl:2016:COLING motivate a more thorough analysis of NMT attention models.
This section backgrounds attention and describes non-recurrent global attention and input-feeding attention models used in the paper.
Both non-recurrent and input-feeding models compute context vector INLINEFORM0, concatenate it with decoder hidden state, and pass it through a non-linearity before softmax.
The models differ in context vector computation; non-recurrent attention compares decoder and encoder hidden states, often by dot product, then applies softmax.
INLINEFORM0 is decoder hidden state at INLINEFORM1, INLINEFORM2 is INLINEFORM3 th encoder hidden state, INLINEFORM4 is source length, and alignment weights compute a weighted sum.
Input-feeding makes context vector INLINEFORM0 aware of previous context INLINEFORM1 by feeding back INLINEFORM2 and using the resulting hidden state instead of INLINEFORM3.
INLINEFORM0 is the stacked LSTM function, INLINEFORM1 is the last generated target word, and INLINEFORM2 is the previous input-feeding network output.
The paper investigates whether higher consistency between attention and alignment leads to better translations, testing the common assumption that attention corresponds to word alignments.
Hard alignments from RWTH German-English dataset are converted to soft alignments using Equation EQREF10, with cross entropy between attention and soft alignment as loss.
INLINEFORM0 is the set of source words aligned to target word INLINEFORM1, and INLINEFORM2 is the number of source words in the set.
After converting hard alignments to soft ones, the attention loss is computed as shown.
INLINEFORM0 is the source sentence, INLINEFORM1 is the alignment link weight, and INLINEFORM3 is the attention weight INLINEFORM4 for source word INLINEFORM5.
The analysis relates translation quality to attention quality using attention loss from Equation EQREF11 and word prediction loss against the reference translation.
INLINEFORM0 is the source sentence, INLINEFORM1 is the target word at INLINEFORM2, INLINEFORM3 is target history, and INLINEFORM4 comes from Equation EQREF2.
Spearman's rank correlation computes the correlation between attention loss and word prediction loss.
INLINEFORM0 and INLINEFORM1 are ranks of attention losses and word prediction losses, INLINEFORM2 is covariance, and INLINEFORM3 and INLINEFORM4 are standard deviations.
If word prediction quality relates to attention-alignment consistency, losses should correlate; Figure FIGREF13 shows “will” and “come” with distributed attention.
Attention concentration is analyzed as another variable by computing the entropy of the attention distribution.
Analysis uses global attention without input-feeding and input-feeding recurrent attention in a unidirectional encoder-decoder NMT system with 4 recurrent layers.
Systems were trained with dimension size of 1,000, batch size of 80, 20 epochs, 30K vocabularies, learning rate 1, gradient norm 5, and dropout 0.3.
Both systems were trained on WMT15 German-to-English training data, with statistics in Table TABREF18 and BLEU scores in Table TABREF17.
Because the analysis uses word-based POS tags and dependency roles, BPE BIBREF13 was not used since it operates at the sub-word level.

AER is reported against RWTH German-English dataset human alignments, with hard alignments from most attended words and GIZA++ automatic alignments symmetrized using grow-diag-final-and refined heuristic.
Table TABREF20 shows the input-feeding system achieves higher BLEU and uses attentions closer to human alignments.
Table TABREF21 compares input-feeding and non-recurrent attention using attention loss from Equation EQREF11 against human alignments, with differences in line with AER.
AER considers only the most attended word, while attention loss considers the entire attention distribution.
Mixed results on optimizing attention with alignments motivate fine-grained analysis using coarse grained universal POS tags BIBREF15 from Table TABREF25.
Figure FIGREF22 shows attention loss varies across POS tags, with NOUN closest to alignments and VERB average attention loss almost two times larger than NOUN.
Figure FIGREF22 shows verbs have smaller average word prediction loss than nouns despite attention being more inconsistent with word alignments.
Spearman's rank correlation between word prediction loss and attention loss is computed by target-side POS tags for the input-feeding model in Figure FIGREF27.
Low verb correlation shows attention beyond aligned words is necessary, while higher noun correlation makes alignment consistency more desirable and explains mixed guided-attention results.
Most target words align to one source word, with average aligned source words of 1.1 for nouns and 1.2 for verbs, motivating attention entropy measurement.
Figure FIGREF28 shows nouns have low attention entropy, explaining closeness to alignments, and high correlation between attention entropy and attention loss for nouns.
Figure FIGREF28 shows verbs have higher attention entropy, while Figure FIGREF32 shows attention concentration is not required when translating into verbs.
Figure FIGREF32 shows low correlation for PRON and PRT, whose distributed attention may reflect deliberate attention to multiple relevant places supported by low word prediction losses.
The study measures average attention paid to aligned words for each POS tag using the percentage of probability mass assigned to aligned words in Table TABREF35.
Less than half of attention goes to alignment points for most POS tags; ParZu parser BIBREF16 parses RWTH data, and Table TABREF33 shows attended dependency roles.
The conclusion states attention agrees with alignment to an extent, varies by mechanism and word type, and alignment training helps nouns but harms verbs.
